This is a difficult question to answer within the abstract. For example a complete socialist system, theoretically at least, would not function on a national basis. It would involve an international cooperative administration to coordinate production and distribution of resources on a global scale. This would be very possible, as many private companies already coordinate distribution on this scale today (for example Fed Ex tracks and coordinates a global distribution system that spans the globe.)

Short of this type of global planned economy, there would be all type of contridiction that would exist as a socialist government tried to extend control over one country or one region.

This process would not be uniform in every country either. For example one critical aspect of consolidating a planned economy would be resolving the contradiction between industrial and agrarian production. This was a major issue in the Soviet Union and China, as industrial power, which was sphere of the economy that the government was trying to grow rapidly, was heavily out matched against the scale of the agrarian economy. This created all sorts of problems as the agrarian workers and small/large estate owners didn't feel that they had any vested interest in the new socialist government and actively tried to sabotage or opt out of it.

But this issue would be diffrent in every country. In the United States or France for example agriculture is almost completely mechinized, with small landowners comprising a fraction of a fraction of agricultural output. However in a country like Venezuela or Kenya mechinization of agriculture is still developing and small landowners are still a sizeable element in the agrarian sector.

I could site more examples but the point is that socialist policies would look different depending on the level of productive capacity in a given region and also upon the stage socialist accumulation we are talking about.
